newsitem.title: PERU: Momentum builds for peaceful end to Peru crisis.
newsitem.headline: Momentum builds for peaceful end to Peru crisis.

text.p: Peruvian rebels and the government have not yet agreed on key points but momentum appeared to be building on Wednesday for an accord to end the 99-day Lima crisis, diplomatic sources said.

The Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) hostage-takers have agreed to fly to Cuban asylum along with some of their 72 captives but the two sides remain apart on the main MRTA demand -- freedom for 450 jailed comrades, the sources said.
That demand, repeatedly rejected by President Alberto Fujimori in the 14-week standoff at the Japanese ambassador's home, is the main obstacle now, they added.
"Asylum seems to be pretty well sewn up," said one diplomat. "The core issue now is what to do about the prisoners. That's the real area of contention."
Official circles in Lima were optimistic on Tuesday that a peaceful solution to Latin America's longest hostage siege was in the offing.
"There really is a certain degree of optimism," Bolivia's acting ambassador, Eloy Avila, told local radio. "We see flexibility on the part of the government and the MRTA."
Bolivian Ambassador Jorge Gumucio is one of the hostages.

"There's a certain momentum building," added one Western diplomat, who requested anonymity. "I mean, what do you do if there's no solution. All that's left after that is the military option, and no one seems to want that."
Sources said asylum is part of a draft deal hammered out by a three-man mediation team, known as the guarantors commission, after separate talks with both sides.

Cuba and the Dominican Republic have offered asylum as part of a broader settlement to end the siege. Rebels initially spurned the idea, saying they wanted to return to the armed struggle after winning release of their comrades, but have since said they could accept asylum for at least some of their number.

"For a long time the talks seemed to be going up and down every day. But now there's progress; there's a mood of optimism," one diplomat said, adding that even if talks went smoothly freedom for hostages could be 10 days to two weeks away.
Despite the most positive mood, there was no confirmation from official quarters that a deal was close.
Fujimori, inaugurating a scenic viewing point on a Lima hilltop, made no reference to crisis talks but called for a "rational solution" and pledged "solidarity" with the hostages.
"May Holy Week be propitious so that respect for peace, life and liberty is imposed. That is what Peru wants," he said.

In the latest of a flurry of meetings, Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent and Red Cross representative Michel Minnig, both guarantors, met the MRTA command on Tuesday inside the residence and then at a safe house outside.
The meeting was also attended by Japanese government observer Terusuke Terada. But all parties left afterward without comment.

"All this does not mean we are at the doorstep of a solution but it does mean we have reached a road that will take us to a solution," Avila said. "We hope that with the next conversations starting on Monday or Tuesday we will have something to celebrate."

About 20 rebels stormed the residence on Dec. 17, 1996, seizing hundreds of hostages, most of whom were freed in the weeks after the takeover. They continue to hold their most prized bargaining chips, including Fujimori's brother, Pedro, the envoys of Japan and Bolivia, and dozens of Japanese diplomats and businessmen.
After the ceremony, Fujimori walked down Cerro San Cristobal, mingling with supporters in Lima's poor Rimac district, but offered few comments on the hostage siege.
Those he met along the way liked the way the Peruvian leader has all but stamped out guerrilla violence in Peru since he first took office in 1990.

"Peru is in a good situation now," said Andres Albier after holding his nine-month-old baby, Rosemary, for Fujimori to kiss. "There used to be a lot of terrorism but (Fujimori) has done what a lot of other presidents were unable to."
